reason: The 2004 expedition led by Tsunemi Kubodera is documented across all six source sites, providing over 20 unique claims with high consensus.
story: For centuries, the giant squid was a myth—the real-life Kraken. Despite being one of the largest invertebrates on Earth with massive eyes, no one had ever seen a live one in its deep-sea home. In 2004, Japanese zoologists Tsunemi Kubodera and Kyoichi Mori changed history. They tracked the movements of the squid’s primary predator, the sperm whale, to a hunting ground 900 meters below the North Pacific. After years of failure, they deployed a baited camera that finally hit the jackpot. A massive 8-meter squid struck the line with surprising aggression, snagging its tentacle on a hook. It fought for over four hours before breaking free, leaving behind a 5.5-meter severed tentacle that was still moving when hauled to the surface. DNA confirmed the find. The Kraken wasn't just a legend; it was a powerful predator finally caught on camera in the dark.
angle: Scientists captured the first-ever photos of a live giant squid by tracking its greatest predator, the sperm whale, to a depth of 900 meters.

claims.claim: The giant squid is the second-largest mollusc and one of the largest invertebrates.
The colossal squid is the only living invertebrate that exceeds the giant squid in size.
Giant squid are widespread, occurring in all of the world's oceans.
Their vertical distribution spans depths from roughly 300 to 1,000 meters.
The first photographs of a live giant squid in its natural habitat were taken on September 30, 2004.
The discovery was made by a team led by Tsunemi Kubodera and Kyoichi Mori.
The images were captured 900 meters beneath the North Pacific Ocean near the Ogasawara Islands.
Researchers located the squid by following the diving patterns of sperm whales.
The team used a baited line with a camera and flash to attract the animal.
A giant squid attacked the lure and snagged a tentacle on a hook.
The squid struggled for over four hours to free itself from the hook.
The squid left behind a severed tentacle measuring 5.5 meters in length.
The severed tentacle was still moving and its suckers could still clutch objects after being hauled aboard.
DNA testing on the recovered tentacle confirmed the specimen was a giant squid.
The 2004 photos showed the squid is a much more aggressive predator than previously thought.
The 2004 specimen was estimated to be approximately 8 meters long.
The giant squid's suckers are lined with sharp, serrated rings of chitin.
Giant squid possess a powerful, parrot-like beak used to shred prey.
Genetic research suggests that only a single species of giant squid exists worldwide.
Sperm whales are the primary predators of adult giant squid.
The first film footage of a live giant squid in its habitat was captured in 2012 by a team including Kubodera.

disputed: The specific bait used in 2004 is reported as cuttlefish in some accounts but as small squid and shrimp in others; a script should refer to it generally as a baited line.

The maximum possible length is debated, with modern scientific estimates around 13 meters while historical accounts claim up to 18.5 meters; attribute the larger size to a historical 19th-century record.
The number of species was historically debated up to 17, but recent DNA evidence supports only one; attribute the single-species finding to recent genetic analysis.
